name: Philidor position (rook and pawn versus rook, third-rank defence)

plans.label: Rook on the sixth, White's king kept off it
plans.description: Park the rook on the defender's third rank and leave it there: the fence keeps the attacking king off the sixth, and without its king in front the pawn cannot make progress.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Third-rank defence', whose success was holding. It is now the set-up that does the holding: Black's rook stands on its third rank — the sixth — and White's king has not reached that rank. The fence being on the board is checkable; that it held to the end is not. Original success note: 'Holding is an outcome and has no structural signature here.'

plans.label: Pawn on the sixth, rook swung to the rear rank
plans.description: The moment the pawn steps onto the defender's third rank the fence has done its work: the rook stands on the far rank behind the pawn, ready to check forever.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Drop to the rear when the pawn advances', whose success was move order. It is now the arrangement the move order produces: White's passed pawn stands on the sixth rank and Black's rook is on the far rank behind it. It cannot say the rook left at the right moment — only that both facts are true together. Original success note: 'The timing — rook leaves the third rank exactly when the pawn arrives — is move order, not a position census.'

plans.label: King stays on the promotion path
plans.description: Keep the defending king in front of the pawn or on its queening square's file; the whole defence assumes the king does not get driven off sideways.

success.note: Black's king stands on the file of White's passed pawn, expressed one file at a time. The earlier note put king geometry outside the vocabulary; a file-restricted quantified region reaches this particular piece of it exactly. It certifies the king is on the promotion path, not that it can stay there.

plans.label: King forward before the pawn
plans.description: Advance the king and force the defending rook to abandon the third rank before touching the pawn; pushing the pawn early is the concession the defence is waiting for.

success.note: Reaching the seventh is progress the arithmetic can see; whether it is a won Lucena depends on the kings, which it cannot see.

plans.label: Plant the king on the sixth rank
plans.description: If the defender abandons the third-rank plan for passive rook placement, plant the king on the sixth rank; passive defence loses exactly where the Philidor set-up holds.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Punish a passive rook', whose success rested on zugzwang. It is now the first half of the plan's own recipe: White's king has reached the sixth rank, which is exactly what the third-rank defence exists to prevent. The zugzwang half is dropped — a static census cannot see whose move it is to lose. Original success note: 'Zugzwang is a to-move property no static census expresses.'

watch: Fires while a passed pawn stands on ranks four to six of the rook-and-pawn-versus-rook census; the defining features — defending king in front of the pawn, rook on the third rank — are king and rook geometry this vocabulary cannot express. Verify on the board.
Extra pawns are not excluded by the census and change the defence; count them.
Colour convention: White is authored as the stronger/attacking side. Mirror the plans when the colours are reversed; the trigger fires only for the White-side census.
typicalMistakes: Abandoning the third rank before the pawn forces it, or one move after — the rook leaves exactly when the pawn arrives.
Defending with side checks from short distance instead of the rear-checking plan.
Letting the attacking king reach the sixth rank without a fight, after which the third-rank fence no longer exists.
As the attacker, pushing the pawn to the sixth early and handing the defender the rear-checking draw.
